clue.text: Blinking hooter is hard to find!

parts.note: a hooter is a bird that hoots
taken as written
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: An exasperated search for a lost car horn that simply cannot be located.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blinking' reads as a mild British curse on the hooter (a car horn); it is the definition, blinking slowly like a bird of the night.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone blinking slowly through large spectacles is said to look like a wise night bird, solemn and peering.

clue.text: Beat vicar and ring up, getting firm with me

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters run from the bottom, so they read backwards

parts.note: Rev, the Reverend, is a vicar's title
O is ring-shaped
Co is short for company, a firm
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone thrashed the vicar and phoned him, being stern with the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring up' reads as phoning; 'up' actually turns round the clergyman and the circle before them.
explanation.definitionFit: To overcome an opponent is to defeat or conquer them, so it means beat in the sense of win against.

clue.text: Timber supplier wanted chimney to have a light in

indicators.note: to have something in is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: lum is a Scottish and northern word for a chimney
taken as written
to burn is to give off light, as a lamp does
completes the phrase 'to have ... in'

explanation.surface: A wood merchant wants a lamp fitted in his chimney.
explanation.walkthrough: LUM is a dialect word a non-British solver may not know: the chimney in Scots. The laburnum is a small tree with yellow flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree yields wood, so any tree can be called a source of lumber in cryptic terms.

clue.text: Country's uplifting tunes about the Fourth of July

indicators.note: lifting a down entry upwards makes its letters read from the bottom
about means surrounding, going round something

parts.note: airs are melodies

indicators.note: the fourth of a word is the letter in fourth position

parts.note: the letter in fourth place of July

explanation.surface: A nation is playing rousing music for American Independence Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Fourth of July' looks like the American holiday; read literally it is the fourth letter of the month's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Syria is a nation in the Middle East bordering Turkey, Iraq and Lebanon.

clue.text: Inside stone front door it rattled

indicators.note: inside tells us one word sits within another word here

parts.note: agate is a banded semi-precious stone
taken as written

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of door

explanation.surface: Someone describes a front door rattling inside a stone house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front door' looks like one thing, the entrance, but 'front' only picks the opening letter of the following word.
explanation.definitionFit: To be rattled is to be flustered or unsettled, a close synonym of nervously disturbed.

clue.text: Waving toy dog, I get people inside — which helps sales!

indicators.note: inside places one group within the other
something waving moves to and fro, so these letters are thrown about

parts.note: letters to be mixed
the public are people at large

explanation.surface: A salesperson waves a toy dog to draw shoppers into the store.
explanation.walkthrough: The mixed letters split round the people word: four before, three after.
explanation.definitionFit: Favourable press attention boosts how many products are bought, so the phrase is what aids trade.

clue.text: Lots of you, once on beaches

parts.note: thou is the old form of you
sands are beaches

explanation.surface: Crowds of people once flocked to the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' marks an archaic word.
explanation.definitionFit: Thousands is an informal way of saying very many, a great number of things.

clue.text: If a drink's wanted, there''s bags in this

definitions.text: If a drink's wanted, there''s bags in this

parts.note: surface reading: plenty, lots of room; setter's reading: small paper sachets of leaves go into the brewing vessel

explanation.walkthrough: 'There's bags' sounds like slang for plenty; it is literal, the sachets of leaves dropped in before the water.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewing vessel with a spout is where leaves or sachets steep in hot water to make a cuppa.

clue.text: Declines to go with the foreign lorry driver

indicators.note: foreign tells us to take the word from another language, here Spanish or French

parts.note: something that declines dies away
el is 'the' in Spanish

explanation.surface: A trucker turns down a job with foreign firms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lorry driver' suggests a person; it is the fuel that drives the engine. A lorry is a British truck.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy-oil fuel powers truck engines, so it is literally what propels the vehicle.

clue.text: Queen holds medal found in fireplace

indicators.note: one thing holding another keeps it within its grasp

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen
the MBE is a British honour awarded as a medal

explanation.surface: The monarch keeps a medal tucked away somewhere in the fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a descriptive phrase rather than a noun: what you might find glowing in a grate.
explanation.definitionFit: A glowing remnant of coal or wood is what remains in a hearth after the fire burns down.

clue.text: Companion wants cool tea, stirred and sweet

parts.note: CH is a Companion of Honour

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: letters to be mixed

explanation.surface: A friend asks for a cold, stirred, sugary tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' seems to describe the tea; it is the definition, a confection.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet in British usage is a confection or candy, and a cocoa bar is a typical example.

clue.text: Time for prayer for church dignitary, one time outside California

indicators.note: outside means surrounding, so the abbreviation sits within the pair

parts.note: a canon is a senior cleric of a cathedral
I is the Roman numeral one
an hour is a period of time
Cal is the old abbreviation for California

explanation.surface: A cleric's schedule allows prayer time while visiting California.
explanation.walkthrough: The one and the time sit on either side of the state abbreviation, giving ICALHOUR after the cleric.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of the fixed daily offices, such as matins or vespers, is a set period for worship.

clue.text: Copper put "rain ruined start of play"

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: something ruined is wrecked out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: letters to be mixed; the quotation mark is surface only

explanation.surface: A policeman reports that wet weather has spoiled the opening of a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is British slang for a police officer, but here it is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: The theatre phrase marks the moment the stage drapes rise and a performance begins.

clue.text: Talked of using pole to dig with

parts.note: S is the South pole
to dig someone is to poke or prod them

explanation.surface: Someone describes using a pole as a digging tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dig' suggests a spade, but it means a jab.
explanation.definitionFit: The past tense of speak, so it means conversed or said something aloud.

clue.text: Armed when going to a funeral?

definitions.text: Armed when going to a funeral?

parts.words: Armed when going to a funeral?
parts.note: surface reading: carrying weapons; setter's reading: what is worn round the upper arm by a mourner

explanation.walkthrough: 'Armed' suggests weapons; read it as 'wearing something on the arm', and the black strip a mourner wears appears.
explanation.definitionFit: A black strip of cloth worn on the sleeve signals grief for someone who has died.

clue.text: Nothing goes on in their camps

definitions.text: Nothing goes on in their camps

parts.words: Nothing goes on in their camps
parts.note: surface reading: the camps are dull, with no activity; setter's reading: nobody puts any clothes on there

explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes on' reads as 'happens'; take it as 'is put on' and the camps become clothing-free resorts.
explanation.definitionFit: Nudists live or holiday without clothes, often at dedicated camps and beaches.

clue.text: Elated, but still after church backing

indicators.note: after places this piece behind the next one
backing means going backwards, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
static means motionless

explanation.surface: A worshipper is overjoyed, yet unmoving, after church support.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like 'nevertheless' after 'but'; it is the adjective meaning motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstatic means overwhelmed with joy, a stronger synonym of very happy and thrilled.

clue.text: Field behind East Street is cut off

indicators.note: behind places this piece after the others

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for East
St is the abbreviation for Street
a range is a field of scope, or an open grazing field

explanation.surface: A field at the back of East Street has been isolated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut off' reads as a description of the field; it is the verb definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange someone is to alienate or separate them from family or friends.

clue.text: Glue with scent is upsetting tiny pets

parts.note: to glue is to stick

indicators.note: upsetting knocks things over and out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: letters to be mixed

explanation.surface: The smell of glue is distressing to small household animals.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'is upsetting' as one verb phrase; 'is' is merely part of the letters to be mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Twig-like phasmids are commonly kept by children in tanks as small, low-maintenance animals.

clue.text: Stands in for Jethro straight away

indicators.note: in means the letters lie inside the following words

parts.note: spans the end of the name and the start of the next word
surface padding completing 'straight away'

explanation.surface: Someone deputises for Jethro at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stands in for' reads as a phrasal verb meaning deputises; split it, and 'Stands' alone is the plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Rostra are raised platforms for speakers, plural of rostrum, so they are stands.

clue.text: Holiday accommodation hired after tea

indicators.note: after places this piece behind the next one

parts.note: cha is slang for tea
a property let is hired out

explanation.surface: A holiday cottage is rented after afternoon tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A wooden mountain cabin or a holiday-camp hut is a common rental lodging for vacationers.

clue.text: An unmarried mother is different

indicators.note: un- strips away 'married', whose standard abbreviation is a single letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A single mum is seen as standing apart from others.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the standard abbreviation for married, so an 'unmarried' word loses its M.
explanation.definitionFit: Something other is distinct or not the same, which is what different means.

clue.text: Where you'll find trees scattered round frozen water

definitions.note: a place, standing for the name of a city

indicators.note: round means placed on either side, enclosing something within
scattered things are strewn about in no order, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the setter's slip: these five letters are meant to supply six, an L included
frozen water is ice

explanation.surface: Directions to a woodland with trees dotted around a frozen pond.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a letter short: the anagram fodder has no L, so the clue as printed cannot quite give the answer. Leicester is an English city in the Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue asks for a location, and this Midlands city is a place in England.

clue.text: About ten engineers turned to go in

indicators.note: turned means facing the other way, so both pieces read backwards
about means surrounding, going round something

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers
taken as written

explanation.surface: Roughly ten engineers reversed direction in order to come inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'approximately'; it says the engineers go round the number, each piece turned.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter is to come or go into a place, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Politician follows everyone into backstreet to see invention

indicators.note: following means coming after, so this piece is placed last
going into something means being placed inside it

parts.note: street is abbreviated ST, and back means it is read the other way
everyone is all
a Tory is a British Conservative politician

explanation.surface: A politician trails a crowd down a back alley to inspect a new gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backstreet' looks like one word, an alley; split it into 'back' and 'street'.
explanation.definitionFit: An invention here is a fabrication, a made-up account too far-fetched to believe.

clue.text: Giant thing in bronze

indicators.note: in places one word within the other

parts.note: bronze is a tan colour
it stands for any thing

explanation.surface: A huge object cast in bronze, like a statue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thing' reads as an object made of the metal; it is just the pronoun standing for any object, and 'bronze' is a colour, not the alloy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were the giant elder gods of Greek myth, so the name stands for any huge figure.

clue.text: One painting lines with great skill

parts.note: one who paints is an artist
RY is railway, and railway lines are its usual crossword sense

explanation.surface: A painter executes lines with great skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' looks like brushstrokes, but it is railway lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Artistry is creative mastery or craftsmanship, high ability in making things.

clue.text: One advising one to leave the Spanish capital when rejected

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: el is Spanish for the

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: Cairo is the capital of Egypt
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A counsellor asks someone to abandon the Spanish capital after being turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Spanish capital' suggests Madrid, but 'the Spanish' is EL and the capital is another city, which loses its I.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece an oracle was a priestess or shrine giving counsel or prophecy to those consulting it.
